title: EPRO: Robust Policy Optimization Through an Imperfect Execution-Policy Predictor
authors: Yibo Wang, Changyi Yang, Yuanxin Liu, Zhaoran Wang
abstract: RL for LLMs often separates rollout generation from policy training. Although the two numerical engines share model parameters, they can induce different policies. This creates a challenge beyond correcting a known training-inference mismatch: during learner updates, the execution policy corresponding to the current parameters cannot be directly observed. We view this as optimizing an unobserved execution policy through an imperfect predictor of its evolution. This perspective raises two fundamental questions: how can we estimate the execution policy's response to learner updates, and how much should we trust that estimate when optimizing the actual execution policy? We introduce Execution-Policy Robust Optimization (EPRO) to address these challenges. Starting from the observed rollout-time execution policy, we use training-policy changes to construct a differentiable predictor of the current execution policy, whose score yields Transported Score Centering (TSC). Our robust-improvement analysis reveals how prediction error limits the magnitude of reliably justified updates. For practical implementation, we introduce Policy Shift as an observable proxy for prediction risk and use Shift-Aware Soft Clipping (SSC) to attenuate risky updates. Across four Qwen3 model settings, EPRO achieves the highest average held-out accuracy among the compared methods on seven mathematical reasoning benchmarks.

infographic.key_insight: EPRO improves LLM reinforcement learning by predicting how learner updates change the unobserved execution policy and tempering updates when that prediction is risky.
infographic.engineering_relevance: EPRO addresses policy mismatches between rollout and training engines that share model parameters but behave differently.
method: Predict the current execution policy from observed rollout behavior and training-policy changes.
Use the predictor’s score to derive Transported Score Centering (TSC).
Use Policy Shift as a prediction-risk proxy and Shift-Aware Soft Clipping (SSC) to attenuate risky updates.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across four Qwen3 model settings, EPRO achieves the highest average held-out accuracy among compared methods on seven mathematical reasoning benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Policy Shift is a proxy for prediction risk; the abstract does not quantify how reliably it tracks execution-policy prediction error.
infographic.paper_title: EPRO: Robust Policy Optimization Through an Imperfect Execution-Policy Predictor

title: U-Statistics-Powered LLM Reasoning
authors: Shijin Gong, Kai Ye, Victor Chernozhukov, Xinyu Zhang, Chengchun Shi
abstract: Since its introduction by DeepSeek, group relative policy optimization (GRPO) has been widely adopted for training large reasoning models and agents, spurring a proliferation of its variants. Yet the group size, a crucial hyperparameter in these GRPO-type algorithms, remains largely chosen by trial and error. Exploiting the U-statistic structure of GRPO's policy gradient, we recast the selection of the group size as a classical statistical problem of variance ratio estimation. This problem is particularly challenging when the denominator of the ratio is small, rendering naive plug-in estimators unstable. To address this challenge, we propose a pessimistic ratio estimator that accounts for the denominator's estimation uncertainty. We characterise the statistical properties of this estimator across three sample-size regimes. Empirically, using %a jackknife-based pessimistic rule on synthetic tasks from Reasoning Gym and real-world benchmarks covering both mathematical reasoning and code generation, we show that our adaptive group size selection reduces the mean squared error of the resulting policy gradient and improves policy optimisation over fixed-group-size baselines, with modest additional computational cost.

infographic.key_insight: The U-statistic structure of GRPO policy gradients turns group-size selection from trial and error into a variance-ratio estimation problem.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Adaptive group sizing can reduce policy-gradient error and improve reasoning-model training over fixed group sizes with modest additional computational cost.
method: Express GRPO group-size selection through policy-gradient variance components.
Use a pessimistic ratio estimator that accounts for denominator uncertainty.
Apply a jackknife-based selection rule and characterize three sample-size regimes.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments on synthetic Reasoning Gym tasks and real-world mathematical reasoning and code-generation benchmarks report lower policy-gradient mean squared error and improved policy optimization.
infographic.watch_item: Near-zero variance-ratio denominators make estimation difficult, so uncertainty handling is crucial for reliable group-size selection.
infographic.paper_title: U-Statistics-Powered LLM Reasoning

title: SGD with Large Learning Rates: General Analysis & Improved Rates
authors: Konstantinos Emmanouilidis, Ziqing Xu, Salma Tarmoun, Lachlan MacDonald, Rene Vidal
abstract: Stochastic Gradient Descent lies at the core of modern machine learning. However its classical analysis typically restricts the stepsize to be below a curvature-dependent stability threshold. Recent developments in deterministic optimization have challenged this paradigm, showing that suitably chosen large stepsizes can not only preserve convergence, but also accelerate Gradient Descent (GD). Whether this phenomenon persists in the presence of stochastic gradient noise has remained an open question (Wu et al., 2024). In this work, we answer this question affirmatively for the cross-entropy loss with linear predictors and two-layer neural networks, establishing an accelerated $\mathcal{O}(T^{-2})$ convergence rate. At the core of our analysis is a fine-grained characterization of the stochastic large-stepsize dynamics. This sharper control of the trajectory further yields tight convergence guarantees within the stable regime, improving existing bounds even in the deterministic setting. Taken together, our results show that the acceleration mechanism induced by large stepsizes survives stochasticity and extends beyond linear models. Numerical experiments demonstrate the benefits of large learning rates in practice.

infographic.key_insight: For cross-entropy loss with linear predictors and two-layer neural networks, suitably chosen large SGD learning rates can preserve convergence and achieve an accelerated O(T^-2) rate despite stochastic gradient noise.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results motivate testing larger learning rates rather than treating classical curvature-based stability thresholds as absolute limits.
method: Characterize stochastic optimization trajectories under large learning rates.
Establish accelerated convergence for cross-entropy with linear and two-layer models.
Use sharper trajectory control to improve stable-regime convergence guarantees, including for deterministic optimization.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments demonstrate practical benefits of large learning rates, but the abstract provides no datasets, benchmark details, or effect sizes.
infographic.watch_item: The guarantees concern specific losses and model classes; arbitrary large learning rates or extensions to deeper networks are not established by the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: SGD with Large Learning Rates: General Analysis & Improved Rates

title: A Calculus Gradient: Child Poverty, Mathematics Preparation, and First-Year College Performance at a Hispanic-Serving University
authors: Juan B. Gutiérrez
abstract: The San Antonio metropolitan area has one of the highest poverty rates among large U.S. metropolitan areas. Within Bexar County, where the city is located, child poverty varies widely across school districts. We link entrants of the city's public research university, a broad-access Hispanic-Serving Institution, to their sending schools and districts, and examine their preparation scores and first-year outcomes. Across the nation's school districts, enrollment in widely taken core courses (Algebra II, Geometry, Biology) shows little relation to child poverty, while enrollment in Calculus and Advanced Placement mathematics and science is far lower where child poverty is higher, nationally and within Bexar County. Among linked entrants, mathematics preparation differs with the school and district. Entrants with stronger mathematics preparation earn higher first-year grades in nearly every subject. Most entrants who do not return after the first year had unsuccessful courses, and mathematics is the largest single source of those outcomes. Among students who change major, mathematics is one of the subjects with grades furthest below their own averages. Within the same course and term, larger mathematics sections go with more unsuccessful outcomes for entrants with lower mathematics preparation, which identifies a hypothesis for testing smaller sections. Recorded between Fall 2014 and Fall 2019, these outcomes offer a reference point for change after the pandemic, test-optional admissions, and generative artificial intelligence. The analysis is reproducible; adapting it elsewhere requires local definitions and linkage validation. All results are associations among the students of one institution; establishing causes would require a designed study.

infographic.key_insight: Higher child poverty is associated with less access to advanced mathematics, while stronger mathematics preparation is associated with better first-year grades across nearly every subject.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For engineering education, mathematics preparation and course design are potential targets for supporting first-year success, though intervention effects remain untested.
method: Link university entrants to sending schools and districts.
Compare course enrollment patterns with district child poverty.
Analyze preparation, grades, return rates, major changes, and mathematics section sizes.
infographic.evidence_signal: Fall 2014–Fall 2019 records from one broad-access Hispanic-Serving university show that mathematics was the largest single source of unsuccessful course outcomes among entrants who did not return after year one.
infographic.watch_item: Findings are associative, not causal; smaller mathematics sections require designed evaluation, and replication requires validated local data linkages.
infographic.paper_title: A Calculus Gradient: Child Poverty, Mathematics Preparation, and First-Year College Performance at a Hispanic-Serving University

title: From the ELBO to Maximum Likelihood: Convergence of Variational Autoencoders for Nonlinear Mixed-Effects Modeling
authors: Jan Rohleff, Johannes Schropp
abstract: Nonlinear mixed-effects (NLME) models are the central statistical models of pharmacometrics, where they support dose selection, individualized dosing and regulatory decisions in drug development. Statistically, NLME modeling is a marginalized likelihood problem. Variational autoencoders (VAEs) solve such problems with a neural network encoder that amortizes the approximation of the intractable posterior distribution, and allow the integration of AI components into NLME modeling. This paper provides the convergence analysis of the VAE-NLME algorithm. First, its version for the evidence lower bound (ELBO) is proven to converge almost surely to the set of stationary points of the ELBO, without assuming that the encoder is trained exactly. Second, the final VAE-NLME algorithm trains the encoder on the ELBO by gradient-based optimization and uses it as proposal for importance-weighted sufficient statistics. It converges almost surely to the set of stationary points of the marginal log-likelihood, without any assumption on the training of the encoder. Thus, it combines the fast gradient-based training of VAEs with the limit of maximum likelihood estimation.

infographic.key_insight: VAE-NLME connects fast encoder training with almost-sure convergence to stationary points of the marginal log-likelihood.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method supports AI-integrated nonlinear mixed-effects modeling for pharmacometric tasks such as dose selection and individualized dosing.
method: Use a neural encoder to approximate intractable NLME posterior distributions.
Establish ELBO stationary-point convergence without requiring exact encoder training.
Use the encoder as an importance-sampling proposal for sufficient statistics to obtain marginal-likelihood stationary-point convergence.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical almost-sure convergence results, but provides no datasets, numerical benchmarks or runtime comparisons.
infographic.watch_item: Stationary-point convergence does not guarantee a global maximum, and the abstract does not establish finite-time accuracy or efficiency.
infographic.paper_title: From the ELBO to Maximum Likelihood: Convergence of Variational Autoencoders for Nonlinear Mixed-Effects Modeling

title: AI-Assisted Auto-formalization for Trustworthy Scientific Computing: Case Studies and Lessons Learned
authors: Mohit Tekriwal, Het Mankad, Naifeng Zhang, Keita Teranishi, Sahil Bhola, Daisuke Uchida
abstract: Agentic AI tools have recently had success in mathematical reasoning. Both general purpose coding agents such as Claude Code and Codex, and specialized mathematics agents such as Aristotle, have been used for formalizing mathematical problems such as Fermat's last theorem, Erdős problems and several IMO level math problems. However, much of these efforts are concentrated in the pure mathematics domain, which benefits from relatively self-contained theorem statements, fixed mathematical representation and extensive support in existing formal libraries. Applied mathematics, on the other hand, presents additional challenges because the source may describe a computational procedure or modeling transformation rather than a declarative theorem. In this work, we present a systematic study of AI-assisted auto-formalization for scientific computing (SC), a domain in applied mathematics central to U.S. Department of Energy applications. Through case studies spanning hierarchical abstraction layers in SC software stack, we evaluate not only whether AI agents can complete numerical proofs, but also where and why they fail across the stack. Our primary contribution is a cross-layer taxonomy of failure modes and an analysis of the form of expert feedback required at each layer to recover mathematical soundness. From these observations, we derive a workflow for recurring proof patterns and practical guidance for using AI agents while preserving mathematical soundness. Our results characterize both the practical value and the current limitations of AI-assisted formalization for trustworthy scientific computing.

infographic.key_insight: Trustworthy AI-assisted formalization in scientific computing requires identifying layer-specific failures and supplying expert feedback to recover mathematical soundness.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The study offers practical guidance for using AI proof agents across scientific computing software layers without treating proof completion alone as evidence of correctness.
method: Study AI-assisted formalization through case studies across scientific computing abstraction layers.
Classify failure modes and the expert feedback needed to recover soundness.
Derive a workflow for recurring proof patterns.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a cross-layer case-study evaluation of numerical proof completion and failures, but provides no quantitative success rates.
infographic.watch_item: Computational procedures and modeling transformations may require expert interpretation beyond the support available in existing formal libraries.
infographic.paper_title: AI-Assisted Auto-formalization for Trustworthy Scientific Computing: Case Studies and Lessons Learned

title: Beyond PINNs: Boundary-Enriched Holomorphic Networks for Laplace Problems
authors: Andrei Vlad Nicula, Kalp Shah, Robert-Stefan Sofroni, Mihnea Andrei Bârsan, Agneya Bhardwaj, Jan Jelínek
abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) solve partial differential equations by penalizing their residual, but this formulation can be difficult to optimize for solutions with singular behaviour. We focus specifically on the two-dimensional Laplace equation, whose strong analytical structure allows the governing equation to be enforced directly in the neural representation. We compare a hybrid harmonic-neural model with a holomorphic neural network whose output is harmonic by construction and therefore requires only boundary training. We further enrich the holomorphic model with singular functions chosen according to the interior angle and boundary conditions at each junction of boundary segments. On six singular benchmarks, the enriched model is the most accurate of the neural models we compare. On the four with a closed-form solution, however, that solution lies in the span of the enrichment terms, and a least-squares fit of these terms alone is exact to rounding error. On Motz's problem and the cracked beam, the neural core reduces the relative error of the recovered leading singular coefficient from about $10^{-2}$, for a least-squares fit with the same four terms, to about $10^{-6}$, and on four variants whose solution has a smooth part outside the span, the network is $4\times10^{4}$ to $2\times10^{7}$ times more accurate than a fit of its singular terms alone; classical least-squares fits with more singular terms, or with harmonic polynomials and rational poles, are more accurate still. Our results demonstrate how exploiting problem-specific analytical structure can provide an alternative to base and residual PINNs for challenging scientific computing problems.

infographic.key_insight: Holomorphic networks enforce the 2D Laplace equation by construction, while boundary-specific singular enrichment improves accuracy near singularities.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For 2D Laplace simulations with corner or boundary-condition singularities, analytical structure enables boundary-only training instead of PDE-residual optimization.
method: Compare hybrid harmonic-neural and holomorphic models with PINN baselines.
Enrich the holomorphic model with singular functions matched to junction angles and boundary conditions.
Benchmark against least-squares fits of singular terms and richer classical harmonic bases.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across six singular benchmarks, the enriched model leads the compared neural models; on Motz’s problem and the cracked beam, its neural core reduces leading singular-coefficient relative error from about 10⁻² to 10⁻⁶ versus a four-term least-squares fit.
infographic.watch_item: Four closed-form benchmarks lie entirely in the enrichment span, and richer classical least-squares bases outperform the network, limiting claims of a neural advantage.
infographic.paper_title: Beyond PINNs: Boundary-Enriched Holomorphic Networks for Laplace Problems

title: Congestion-Aware Adaptive Routing for LLM Classification
authors: Yuan Guo, Stefanus Jasin, Chen-An Lin
abstract: Organizations use large language models (LLMs) to classify jobs that differ in uncertainty and the cost of errors. Querying additional models may improve accuracy, but it also incurs fees and increases congestion at shared servers. We study congestion-aware adaptive routing (CAAR) policies that adapt model selection and stopping decisions to observed outputs while accounting for the steady-state congestion they generate. The objective is to minimize the long-run average cost of misclassification penalties, query fees, and holding costs. We can represent CAAR policies as a mixture of decision trees, and derive exact holding costs for first-come-first-served servers with exponential service times and processor-sharing servers with general service times. We formulate a convex optimization problem with unique optimal model loads. Congestion prices capture the marginal system-wide holding costs of additional queries and guide routing and stopping decisions through a Bayesian dynamic program. We characterize optimal stopping decisions and identify models whose information does not justify their cost. A column-generation algorithm computes optimal CAAR policies and provides an explicit optimality-gap bound. We also bound the additional cost of limiting cascade depth relative to full-depth CAAR. Finally, under a common query-depth limit, cascades with a predetermined model order can be arbitrarily more costly than optimal CAAR, even when the order is randomized and stopping decisions adapt to observed outputs. Numerical experiments distinguish the benefits of adaptive model selection and congestion-aware design.

infographic.key_insight: Adapting which LLM to query next—and when to stop—while accounting for congestion can reduce total classification costs compared with fixed-order cascades.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Shared LLM classification services can balance error penalties, query fees, and waiting costs by routing jobs using observed outputs and congestion prices.
method: Represent adaptive routing policies as mixtures of decision trees and derive holding costs for specified queueing models.
Optimize model loads with a convex formulation and use congestion prices in a Bayesian routing-and-stopping dynamic program.
Compute policies through column generation with explicit optimality-gap and cascade-depth bounds.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports numerical experiments separating the benefits of adaptive model selection and congestion-aware design, but gives no datasets or quantitative results.
infographic.watch_item: Exact holding-cost results rely on specified queueing assumptions; deployments with different service dynamics need validation.
infographic.paper_title: Congestion-Aware Adaptive Routing for LLM Classification

title: Convergence and error analysis of problem-independent machine learning (PIML) with linear completeness
authors: Ke Tan, Chong-Jun Li, Xu Guo
abstract: Problem-independent machine learning (PIML) is an effective computational approach that combines the finite element method with machine learning. PIML uses neural networks to learn the mapping from material distributions or element geometries to the numerical shape functions of substructures. This approach avoids repeated computation while preserving the conformity of the underlying finite element discretization, thereby significantly improving the efficiency of substructure-based finite element analysis. However, existing studies on PIML have primarily focused on numerical accuracy and computational efficiency, while rigorous theoretical analyses of its approximation errors are still limited. In this paper, we establish an error analysis framework for PIML from a classical finite element perspective, in which the numerical error is bounded in terms of the finite element discretization error and the network generalization error. Our analysis shows that, when only rigid-body displacement invariance is enforced, the resulting error estimate contains a learning-induced term that does not necessarily decrease under mesh refinement. To ensure convergence, we propose an improved PIML scheme with linear completeness. By using linear displacement field constraints to reconstruct the corresponding columns of the transition matrix, we ensure that the resulting numerical shape-function space contains the space of linear polynomials. We derive error estimates and establish convergence results of the improved scheme in the H1 and L2 norms. Numerical experiments verify the theoretical results and demonstrate that the improved PIML achieves optimal convergence rates, good generalization performance, and numerical stability.

infographic.key_insight: Enforcing linear completeness in PIML removes a key obstacle to mesh-refinement convergence and enables rigorous H1- and L2-norm error estimates.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports efficient substructure-based finite element analysis by learning reusable numerical shape functions while preserving finite element conformity.
method: Bound PIML error using finite element discretization error and network generalization error.
Identify a learning-induced error term that need not decrease under mesh refinement when only rigid-body displacement invariance is enforced.
Reconstruct transition-matrix columns using linear displacement constraints so the numerical shape-function space contains linear polynomials.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments reported in the abstract verify the theory and demonstrate optimal convergence rates, good generalization, and numerical stability.
infographic.watch_item: Linear completeness requires explicit constraint enforcement, and total error still depends on network generalization; the abstract does not quantify performance on unseen geometries or materials.
infographic.paper_title: Convergence and error analysis of problem-independent machine learning (PIML) with linear completeness

title: Boiling Down Uncertainty: Deep Generative Scenario Search with Decision-Guided Evolution Strategies for Two-Stage Stochastic Optimization
authors: Atefeh Hemmati Golsefidi, David Pisinger
abstract: One of the most common models for handling uncertainty is two-stage stochastic programming. Choosing the right number of scenarios is a trade-off between the uncertainty that can be represented and computational cost. A recent method, Deep Generative Scenario Search, generates synthetic scenarios and improves them by learning from the decisions they induce. The original approach used a black-box gradient estimate, since decisions are piecewise constant across scenarios. This paper provides the missing analytical foundation by deriving the gradient in closed form from recourse duality and an adjoint solve of the regularized reduced problem. The decision-focused direction, with a heuristic direction as a backup when duals are unavailable, defines the sampling subspace of a guided evolution strategy rather than being used as a direct update. For any guiding subspace, the expected update is a descent direction of the smoothed objective, so an inaccurate guide adds variance while the expected step still descends. For six problem families, both guided estimators outperform the baseline. The decision-focused version reduces the mean gap by three-quarters, and on the two families with the most integer variables the reduced sets beat the exact solver's two-hour incumbent in most runs, using a fifth of the time.

infographic.key_insight: Analytical decision-focused gradients guide evolutionary search for compact synthetic scenario sets, improving two-stage stochastic optimization without requiring direct gradient updates.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Smaller, decision-aware scenario sets can reduce computational cost while preserving solution quality in optimization under uncertainty.
method: Derive a closed-form gradient using recourse duality and an adjoint solve of the regularized reduced problem.
Use decision-focused directions—or heuristic backups when duals are unavailable—to guide the evolution strategy’s sampling subspace.
Guarantee expected descent of the smoothed objective for any guiding subspace; inaccurate guidance adds variance.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across six problem families, both guided estimators outperform the baseline; decision-focused guidance cuts the mean gap by three-quarters, and on the two most integer-heavy families, reduced sets beat the exact solver’s two-hour incumbent in most runs using one-fifth of the time.
infographic.watch_item: The descent guarantee concerns the expected update on a smoothed objective, not every sampled step or global optimality.
infographic.paper_title: Boiling Down Uncertainty: Deep Generative Scenario Search with Decision-Guided Evolution Strategies for Two-Stage Stochastic Optimization

title: Interactive Neural Computers
authors: Ross Murphy, Marcel Hedman, Gabriel Brostow
abstract: Computers and their interfaces are usually treated as fixed, so a person, or increasingly an AI agent, must adapt to whatever the operating system presents. This is limiting when someone needs a different workflow, or an interface suited to hands-free use or a disability. We explore an overlooked alternative. Rather than training an agent to operate an existing computer, we train a generative model to be the computer, predicting each next screen from past screens and the user's mouse and keyboard actions. Treating a desktop as an interactive world model raises problems that natural-video world models largely avoid. Without a camera pose to index memory, the model must remember content that has left the screen without any geometric cues. Arithmetic in a terminal has to be exactly right, not merely plausible. Small interface text must also stay legible at interactive frame rates. Our Interactive Neural Computer is structured like a Neural Turing Machine and starts to address these problems with three modules trained end to end from pixels and actions. A surprise-gated slot memory, supervised by latent next-frame prediction (MEMORY-JEPA), stores what is off screen. An exploratory query bridge brings in the reasoning of a pretrained VLM, and a residual renderer predicts only the latent changes between frames. In long closed-loop rollouts, our model recalls occluded files in 64.2% of trials (chance is 33.3%), compared with at most 56.0% for recurrent and sliding-window baselines. It also raises terminal-text OCR accuracy from 1.3% to 50.1%. Finally, because the memory is explicit, it can be transplanted at test time to causally change what the model renders.

infographic.key_insight: Interactive Neural Computers learn to generate the next desktop screen from prior screens and user actions, modeling the computer itself rather than an agent that operates it.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Generative desktop models could enable adaptable workflows and accessible interfaces, provided they can reliably preserve state, compute exactly, and render readable text.
method: Train a Neural Turing Machine–style architecture end to end from pixels and actions.
Store off-screen content with surprise-gated slot memory supervised by latent next-frame prediction (MEMORY-JEPA).
Connect pretrained VLM reasoning through an exploratory query bridge and render only latent changes between frames.
infographic.evidence_signal: In long closed-loop rollouts, occluded-file recall reached 64.2% versus at most 56.0% for recurrent and sliding-window baselines (33.3% chance), while terminal-text OCR accuracy rose from 1.3% to 50.1%.
infographic.watch_item: Exact arithmetic remains a requirement rather than a demonstrated result in the abstract, and 50.1% terminal-text OCR accuracy leaves substantial reliability concerns.
infographic.paper_title: Interactive Neural Computers

title: Agentic Discovery of Simple Symbolic Inventory Policies
authors: Xi Chen, Yuze Chen, Baichuan Mo, Jie Ying, Yuan Zhou
abstract: Designing simple inventory policies becomes increasingly difficult as operational features and system configurations expand. We develop an Agentic Inventory-Policy Discovery System based on explicitly defined simple operational formula (SOF) policy and template classes. Large language models (LLMs) revise symbolic structures, while a numerical engine fits parameters separately for each instance and evaluates the induced policies. Multicriteria parent selection, state-specific operational diagnostics, and reusable symbolic motifs guide structural evolution. A three-stage progression develops shared templates across instances and configurations with varying state dimensions. Experiments on 15,600 instances spanning 50 demand distributions cover lead times, perishability, their combination, and lead times with limited customer patience. The discovered templates improve aggregate empirical performance over evaluated SOF benchmarks and are competitive with policies requiring more elaborate online computations. For a lost-sales system with a three-period lead time, we develop an average-cost decomposition and prove that, under specified demand and cost conditions, a capped dual-shortfall specialization of a discovered policy strictly outperforms every policy in the considered capped base-stock benchmark class. This analysis links the performance advantage to the discovered replenishment mechanism. Together, these results highlight the potential of agentic discovery to generate simple inventory policies with strong empirical performance and identify operational mechanisms amenable to rigorous theoretical analysis.

infographic.key_insight: An agentic system discovers simple symbolic inventory policies by separating LLM-driven formula design from numerical parameter fitting.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Compact replenishment formulas could improve inventory decisions across operational settings without elaborate online computations.
method: LLMs revise symbolic policies within explicitly defined formula and template classes.
A numerical engine fits parameters per instance and evaluates policy performance.
Multicriteria selection, operational diagnostics, and reusable motifs guide a three-stage search for shared templates.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 15,600 instances spanning 50 demand distributions, discovered templates improve aggregate empirical performance over evaluated simple-formula benchmarks; a conditional theorem establishes strict superiority over a specified capped base-stock class.
infographic.watch_item: The theoretical guarantee applies only to a specific three-period lead-time setting under stated demand and cost conditions, and deployment still requires instance-specific parameter fitting.
infographic.paper_title: Agentic Discovery of Simple Symbolic Inventory Policies

title: A statistical measure of trust in generative AI
authors: Alina Ermilova, Valeria Yakupova, Nikita Sushko, Andrey Lovyagin, George Ovchinnikov, Maksim G. Sharaev
abstract: Trustworthiness is a crucial issue for generative AI, as modern models can produce convincing and confident responses even when their outputs are incomplete, unsupported, or wrong. The frequent absence of ground-truth knowledge or labels complicates verification of generative AI outputs. To address this issue, we propose a trustworthiness framework grounded in model-internal confidence calibrated against an external expert reference. We estimate per-token trustworthiness of a student generative model as the statistical typicality of each generated token relative to an expert model's distribution, where the expert is used as a distributional reference rather than as a source of factual verification labels. To this end, we introduce an AI ontology calibrator that leverages the student model's internal latent features and token-level output statistics to compute expert-reference acceptance scores. Combined with traditional token-level confidence, entropy, and perplexity statistics, calibrator scores yield a compact set of $15$ response-level indicators for correctness classification. Evaluated across BF program generation, mathematical problem solving, and medical question answering, combined calibrator and traditional indicators provide complementary reliability signal which could be used to build detectors of untrustworthy outputs and hallucinations. Remarkably, our experiments show that these detectors are transferable across domains, although transferability is not always symmetric.

infographic.key_insight: Token-level statistical typicality against an expert model provides a trust signal that complements a generative model’s own confidence.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Combining expert-reference scores with conventional uncertainty statistics can support detectors of unreliable generated code, mathematical solutions, and medical answers.
method: Use an expert model’s token distribution as a reference, not as factual ground truth.
Train an AI ontology calibrator using student-model latent features and token-level statistics to estimate expert-reference acceptance scores.
Aggregate calibrator scores, confidence, entropy, and perplexity into 15 response-level indicators for correctness classification.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluations on BF program generation, mathematical problem solving, and medical question answering found complementary reliability signals and cross-domain detector transfer, though transfer was not always symmetric.
infographic.watch_item: Expert-reference typicality does not establish factual correctness, and transfer reliability may depend on the source and target domains.
infographic.paper_title: A statistical measure of trust in generative AI

title: Hierarchical randomized neural networks for efficiently and accurately finding multiple solutions of semilinear elliptic equations
authors: Jingying Hu, Jiao Li, Yufeng Xu, Jinyong Ying
abstract: Being able to find multiple solutions of a semilinear elliptic equation is a fundamental problem in scientific computing. In this paper, fully taking the advantages of randomized neural networks, we propose a new efficient and accurate method for identifying potentially as many solutions as possible. The new method is constructed from three aspects--initialization, optimization, a technique for acceleration and improving accuracy, two of which are innovative developments. Firstly, based on the basis functions of a randomized network and the sampling points, a characteristic matrix is introduced so that its singular value decomposition can be used to determine weakly variant search directions, followed by a newly developed algorithm to generate effective initial candidates. Then the good deflated Gauss-Newton method [see {\em A. Riley, et al., SIAM Journal on Scientific Computing 47~(5) (2025) A2963-A2987}] using an exponential deflation operator is adapted as the optimization to search for all multiple solutions. Local error estimate of a particular solution under some proper condition is given in terms of the neurons in the hidden layer and the sampling points for this newly designed method. Furthermore, to accelerate the computation and improve the solution accuracy, a new multilevel method based on hierarchical networks is designed. Without using any {\em a priori} information, several numerical tests show together with the multilevel method, the new method can not only accurately find multiple solutions with relative errors reaching $10^{-16}$ only in less than one-tenth computational cost for the best case, but also preserve the inherent symmetries of multiple solutions.

infographic.key_insight: Hierarchical randomized neural networks combine targeted initialization, deflated optimization, and multilevel refinement to find multiple solutions of semilinear elliptic equations efficiently and accurately.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could help computational engineers identify distinct solution branches without prior knowledge of the solutions.
method: Use an SVD of a characteristic matrix built from network basis functions and sampling points to generate effective initial candidates.
Apply good deflated Gauss–Newton optimization with exponential deflation to search for distinct solutions.
Refine through hierarchical network levels to accelerate computation and improve accuracy.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical tests report relative errors reaching 10^-16, preservation of solution symmetries, and, in the best case, less than one-tenth of the comparison computational cost.
infographic.watch_item: The reported numerical results do not guarantee finding every solution, and the local error estimate requires additional conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Hierarchical randomized neural networks for efficiently and accurately finding multiple solutions of semilinear elliptic equations

title: NABLA: A Noise-Adaptive Blockwise Left-Right Preconditioning Algorithm for Stochastic Optimization
authors: Yanlin Li, Ganzhao Yuan
abstract: We propose NABLA, a noise-adaptive blockwise left-right preconditioning algorithm for mini-batch stochastic nonconvex optimization. NABLA combines an exponential moving average of stochastic gradients with block-diagonal row and column preconditioners constructed from matrix-valued second-moment statistics. Unlike conventional matrix-preconditioned methods that use fixed decay parameters, NABLA adjusts the second-moment averaging coefficient through a closed-loop feedback rule determined by the cumulative stochastic-gradient energy and its running average. The first-moment coefficient remains fixed, allowing the trajectory-dependent adaptation to act directly on the structured preconditioners. The resulting method is horizon-free, requires no prior knowledge of the noise level, and automatically adjusts the memory of its second-moment estimators to the observed optimization dynamics. Under standard lower boundedness, smoothness, unbiasedness, bounded-variance, and spectral-boundedness assumptions, we establish uniform stability and variation bounds for the time-varying block preconditioners and control their interaction with momentum estimation and parameter updates. These results yield the noise-adaptive stationarity guarantee $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{-1/2}+σ^{1/2}T^{-1/4})$, which automatically reduces to the nearly deterministic $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{-1/2})$ rate when the stochastic-gradient noise vanishes. NABLA therefore provides a principled approach to combining closed-loop trajectory feedback with memory-efficient structured matrix preconditioning.

infographic.key_insight: NABLA adapts the memory of structured matrix preconditioners to observed gradient dynamics, yielding a noise-adaptive convergence guarantee without prior knowledge of the noise level.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Block-diagonal row and column preconditioning offers a memory-efficient approach to mini-batch optimization with automatically adjusted second-moment averaging.
method: Combine fixed-coefficient gradient momentum with blockwise left-right matrix preconditioning.
Construct row and column preconditioners from matrix-valued second-moment statistics.
Adjust second-moment averaging through feedback from cumulative stochastic-gradient energy and its running average.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports theoretical stability and stationarity guarantees of Õ(T^(-1/2) + σ^(1/2)T^(-1/4)), but provides no empirical benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: The guarantees require spectral-boundedness and other standard assumptions; practical matrix-update overhead is not evaluated in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: NABLA: A Noise-Adaptive Blockwise Left-Right Preconditioning Algorithm for Stochastic Optimization

title: From Horner's rule to neural networks
authors: Lorenzo Pareschi
abstract: Horner's rule is usually taught as an efficient algorithm for evaluating a polynomial. Read as a recurrence, however, it is also a small computational graph: an input is propagated through intermediate states, while parameters enter locally. This note follows that elementary observation from polynomial evaluation to polynomial fitting. The equation $Va\simeq y$ then unifies least-squares approximation, interpolation and overparametrisation as different regimes of a fixed representation. Neural networks are introduced as the next step: the representation itself becomes parametrised and is learned from data. The purpose is pedagogical rather than encyclopaedic. It offers a numerical route into machine learning, using approximation, linear algebra and optimisation as familiar entry points.

infographic.key_insight: Horner’s rule connects polynomial evaluation to neural networks by viewing computation as a graph, then moving from fixed polynomial features to learned representations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This numerical perspective gives engineers a familiar route from approximation and linear algebra to machine learning.
method: Interpret Horner’s recurrence as a computational graph with intermediate states and local parameters.
Use Va ≈ y to connect polynomial least squares, interpolation and overparametrisation.
Introduce neural networks as models whose representations are parametrised and learned from data.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract describes a pedagogical development, with no datasets, numerical benchmarks or empirical performance results reported.
infographic.watch_item: The conceptual connection does not establish when learned representations outperform fixed polynomial bases.
infographic.paper_title: From Horner's rule to neural networks

title: KKT Atlas: Learning Low-Dimensional Local Scenario Models for Contextual Stochastic Optimization
authors: Zhengzhong Ricky You, Baichuan Mo, Yuan Zhou, Jinhua Zhao, Zuo-Jun Max Shen
abstract: In contextual stochastic optimization, integrated learning trains conditional models on operational loss, but repeatedly solving stochastic programs with many scenarios is costly. We propose KKT Atlas, which partitions contexts into local charts and identifies a low-dimensional subspace per chart from decision gradients of the scenario cost. It generates shared scenarios by jointly fitting subspace coordinates and context-dependent probabilities. We show that one more scenario than the subspace dimension suffices to approximate the conditional Karush-Kuhn-Tucker optimality condition under regularity conditions, yielding decision and risk bounds under local strong convexity, with generalization error scaling with the compact parameter dimension. On three synthetic problems, Atlas uses 4-18 scenarios per decision versus 500 for direct-solve full-support integrated learning. It attains comparable or lower risk with about $4$-$23\times$ construction and $13$-$61\times$ batch deployment speedups. Atlas also achieves lower risk than clustering-based reduction at matched support budgets. In real-world European grid reserve commitment, Atlas compresses 728 scenarios to 8-9, cutting construction and deployment times by factors of about 4 and 3 relative to full-support integrated learning. Its loss is lowest over 11 quarters and, over 17 later quarters with fixed settings, slightly higher than with full-support integrated learning and significantly lower than with the remaining benchmarks.

infographic.key_insight: KKT Atlas learns compact local scenario models that preserve decision-relevant optimality conditions instead of approximating the full uncertainty distribution.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It reduces the cost of training and deploying contextual stochastic optimizers while maintaining competitive operational risk.
method: Partition contexts into local charts and learn low-dimensional subspaces from scenario-cost decision gradients.
Jointly fit shared scenario coordinates and context-dependent probabilities.
Under regularity conditions, use one more scenario than the subspace dimension to approximate conditional KKT optimality.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across three synthetic problems, Atlas uses 4–18 scenarios versus 500, with comparable or lower risk and 13–61× faster batch deployment; European grid tests compress 728 scenarios to 8–9.
infographic.watch_item: Decision and risk bounds require local strong convexity; on 17 later grid quarters, Atlas had slightly higher loss than full-support integrated learning.
infographic.paper_title: KKT Atlas: Learning Low-Dimensional Local Scenario Models for Contextual Stochastic Optimization

title: How Far Apart Are Two Proofs? Measuring Proof Dissimilarity in a Proof Kernel and in Lean/Mathlib
authors: Nikolaos Nikolaou
abstract: We now live in the age of machine-generated mathematics: AI systems produce research-level proofs faster than the human mathematical community can read them. Verification is only part of the challenge. We also need to know whether a "new proof" is indeed new, whether a thousand generated proofs contain one idea or many, and where each sits relative to human mathematics. All of these require measuring distances between proofs. Following Hilbert's 24th problem and the identity-of-proofs problem, we ask how far apart two proofs of one theorem are, and what shape the proof space they inhabit has. We define 19 dissimilarity measures in 6 families (syntactic, structural, dependency & resource, semantic, information-theoretic, higher-categorical) and 10 desirable properties, which we argue are the conditions for safely optimising a measure. In a Curry-Howard kernel, 5 machine-checked proofs that the primes are infinite show that raw syntax cannot tell a rewrite from a new argument, that dependency-based and structural measures reproduce the intuitive ordering (Euclid rewritten < Goldbach < Furstenberg), and that semantic measures invert it: Furstenberg's topological proof produces exactly Euclid's witness. A replication in Lean 4/Mathlib (3 theorems, 19 proofs, 18 measures) confirms that dependency-closure measures track intuition best, and shows that equality of normal forms never holds between differently written versions of the same argument, that proofs by citation look unlike the arguments they cite, and that proof irrelevance cannot distinguish any two proofs. We argue for reporting dissimilarity as a multi-level profile, extend the measures to proofs of different theorems, and discuss uses, from detecting duplicated AI proofs and orchestrating prover agents to interpreting AI proofs via their nearest human-understandable counterparts. Code, Lean sources and data are released.

infographic.key_insight: Proof novelty depends on what is measured: dependency-based distances best match intuitive differences, while semantic measures can identify the same witness in very different arguments.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Multi-level proof dissimilarity profiles could help deduplicate AI-generated proofs, coordinate prover agents, and connect unfamiliar proofs to human-understandable arguments.
method: Define 19 dissimilarity measures across 6 families and propose 10 desirable properties.
Compare syntactic, structural, dependency, semantic, information-theoretic, and higher-categorical views of proofs.
Evaluate in a Curry–Howard kernel and replicate in Lean 4/Mathlib.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation covers 5 kernel-checked proofs of infinitely many primes and a Lean/Mathlib replication with 3 theorems, 19 proofs, and 18 measures; dependency-closure measures track intuition best.
infographic.watch_item: The evaluation is small, and citation-based proofs can look unlike the arguments they cite, complicating automated novelty judgments.
infographic.paper_title: How Far Apart Are Two Proofs? Measuring Proof Dissimilarity in a Proof Kernel and in Lean/Mathlib

title: Online Statistical Inference for Derivative-Free Constrained Stochastic Optimization
authors: Jianliang Ye, Sen Na
abstract: We study statistical inference for nonlinear equality-constrained stochastic optimization problems in settings where derivative information is unavailable or expensive to obtain. While recent advances in stochastic sequential quadratic programming (SSQP) have enabled efficient online optimization, existing methods either rely on gradient information or suffer from high computational costs. To address these limitations, we develop a sketched derivative-free SSQP (SDF-SSQP) method that simultaneously achieves computational efficiency and valid statistical inference. By leveraging randomized sketching, the proposed method reduces the per-iteration computational cost to $O((d+m)^2)$, where $d$ is the dimension of the decision variable and $m$ is the number of constraints, making it well suited for large-scale problems. To overcome the challenges that both sketching and zeroth-order approximations introduce for statistical inference, we adopt a random-scaling approach that eliminates the need for explicit estimation of the asymptotic covariance matrix. We establish the asymptotic normality of the averaged primal--dual iterates and construct a self-normalized statistic that is asymptotically pivotal. The resulting inference procedure is fully online, requires neither covariance estimation nor matrix inversion, and incurs an additional per-iteration cost of the same order as that of the optimization update. Numerical experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method in terms of both optimization performance and statistical inference accuracy.

infographic.key_insight: SDF-SSQP combines derivative-free constrained stochastic optimization with online statistical inference at O((d+m)^2) per-iteration cost.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method targets large-scale nonlinear equality-constrained problems where derivatives are unavailable or costly, with d decision variables and m constraints.
method: Use randomized sketching in derivative-free stochastic sequential quadratic programming.
Establish asymptotic normality for averaged primal–dual iterates.
Apply random scaling for self-normalized inference without explicit covariance estimation or matrix inversion.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments report effective optimization and accurate statistical inference, but the abstract gives no benchmarks or quantitative results.
infographic.watch_item: Inference guarantees are asymptotic; finite-sample reliability and sensitivity to sketching and zeroth-order approximation choices require evaluation.
infographic.paper_title: Online Statistical Inference for Derivative-Free Constrained Stochastic Optimization

title: Notes on Generative AI for Mathematical Research
authors: Shurui Liu
abstract: These notes describe how generative AI is now used to solve and to check research-level mathematics, with a focus on agents and their harnesses. For the proving agents Rethlas, Danus, and Pharos and the verification agent OSVerify, we explain the design principles, compare each with its base model, present case studies, and show how to use and contribute to them. We also briefly review the history of AI for mathematics and the community's reactions to it.

infographic.key_insight: Generative AI agents and their harnesses are being used both to solve and to check research-level mathematics.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Agent and harness design provides a framework for integrating AI-assisted proof generation and verification into mathematical research workflows.
method: Explain design principles for proving agents Rethlas, Danus, and Pharos and verification agent OSVerify.
Compare each agent with its base model and present case studies.
Provide guidance on using and contributing to the agents.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract describes base-model comparisons and case studies but reports no quantitative results or evaluation details.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish verification guarantees, so agent-checked arguments should not be assumed formally certified.
